items.title: I-70 Watkins–Bennett lane closures (holiday travel day)
items.caption:
Heading out on I-70 for the holiday? CDOT crews are installing median cable barriers between Watkins and Bennett.

What to expect:
• Weekdays, 9 a.m.–5 p.m.: one westbound lane and the eastbound shoulder closed
• Saturdays, 7 a.m.–6 p.m.: one lane closed in each direction, plus the westbound shoulder
• Construction trucks entering and leaving the closed left lanes

The work zone runs 13.8 miles, from about two miles east of Exit 292 (Airpark Rd.) to two miles east of Exit 306 (Kiowa-Bennett). CDOT doesn't expect big delays but says to plan extra time. The project is expected to wrap up by late March 2027. Check COtrip.org for real-time lane closures.

Thanks to CDOT and Sentinel Colorado for the details. Slow down in the cone zone and safe travels.

#I70 #Bennett #Watkins #ColoradoRoads #QuintValleyNews

items.title: CO 86 Kiowa Creek bridge replacement (+ the one gratitude line)
items.caption:
Happy Thanksgiving from Quint Valley News. If your plans take you through Kiowa this weekend, the CO 86 bridge replacement at Kiowa Creek is still on CDOT's schedule through winter 2026.

CDOT says to expect:
• Traffic shifts and reduced speeds through the work zone
• A temporary shoofly alignment that keeps traffic moving while the bridge is replaced
• A 12-foot width limit for traffic crossing the bridge while construction is active. Trucks and oversized loads should use another route.

Construction began March 9, 2026. CDOT notes the work is weather-dependent and subject to change, so check COtrip.org before you go. The Town of Kiowa says weekly project updates go out every Friday.

Thanks to CDOT and the Town of Kiowa for keeping folks posted. Today we're grateful for the neighbors out here who show up for each other.

#Kiowa #ElbertCounty #CO86 #QuintValleyNews

items.title: Harbor News Through Time: The Purdy Bridge (1937)
items.caption:
Gig Harbor Through Time: The Purdy Bridge.

The Purdy Bridge was completed on Sept. 29, 1937, over the channel between Henderson Bay and Burley Lagoon. At the time it was considered the longest bridge of its kind: a reinforced-concrete box girder, a design common in Europe but rare in America. Engineer Homer Hadley suggested the design.

It runs 550 feet end to end over five spans, with a 190-foot center span, and it's the fourth bridge at this spot. Pierce County built the first one, a wooden bridge with a swing span, in 1892. Today it's on the National Register of Historic Places.

Photo: Historic American Engineering Record, HAER WA-101, Library of Congress (public domain). This is a later survey photo, not a 1937 image.
Source: HistoryLink.org Essay 7133, https://www.historylink.org/File/7133
Source: Library of Congress, HAER WA-101 (Purdy Bridge), https://www.loc.gov/item/wa0455/

items.title: Harbor News Through Time: The Fox Island Bridge (1954)
items.caption:
Gig Harbor Through Time: The Fox Island Bridge.

On Aug. 28, 1954, Gov. Arthur B. Langlie cut the ribbon on the bridge across Hale Passage, and Fox Island traded the ferry for a road to the mainland. The Washington State Toll Bridge Authority built the 1,981-foot span, and it ran as a toll bridge until 1965. Seventy-two years later, it's still the island's road to the mainland.

Bonus fact: the island itself was named in 1841, during the Wilkes Expedition, for Dr. J.L. Fox, an assistant surgeon on the voyage.

Photo: "FI-Bridge 1" by Hedwig in Washington, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0 (cropped and toned), https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:FI-Bridge_1.jpg
Source: Washington State Archives, Guide to the Records of the Washington State Toll Bridge Authority, https://www.sos.wa.gov/sites/default/files/2022-05/Washington-Toll-Bridge-Authority-1937-1977.pdf
Source: Tacoma Public Library Northwest Room, Richards Studio D79525-3 (Fox Island bridge construction, 1953), https://tpl.accesstomemory.org/d79525-3
Source: Pierce County, Gig Harbor Community Plan (history of the Peninsula and Fox Island), https://www.piercecountywa.gov/DocumentCenter/View/38486/ADOPTED-Gig-Harbor-Community-Plan
Source: The Bridge Guy, "What's up with the Fox Island Bridge?", https://thebridgeguy.org/2022/02/whats-up-with-the-fox-island-bridge/

items.title: Harbor News Through Time: Born From the Flames (Fire District No. 5, 1945)
items.caption:
Gig Harbor Through Time: Born From the Flames.

In the spring of 1944, a fire tore through the north-end waterfront and destroyed several businesses. Gig Harbor had no organized fire department, so neighbors led by John Finholm got together and started one.

By January 1945, Pierce County Fire Protection District No. 5 was official, an all-volunteer department. The first career hire came in 1973. Today that department is Gig Harbor Fire & Medic One, covering about 54 square miles of the Peninsula, Fox Island and Raft Island from nine stations.

Eighty-one years later, it's still neighbors looking out for neighbors. Thank you to every firefighter and medic, volunteer and career, who has answered the call out here.

Graphic: Harbor News typographic illustration (no photo).
